stem: On corneal examination, Kayser-Fleischer rings are often present in patients with
explanation: Wilson disease is a genetic disorder of copper metabolism that leads to copper accumulation in various organs, primarily the liver and brain. The clinical symptoms are a result of organ dysfunction due to the direct or indirect effects of copper accumulation. Wilson disease is typically described as a hepato-neurological disease, with focus on signs of liver disease and extrapyramidal symptoms (e.g. wing-beating tremor and dystonia). Copper accumulates in multiple organs over the course of the disease, leading to a variety of clinical manifestations, including neurologic (40-50% at diagnosis), psychiatric (10-25% at diagnosis, and up to 100% over the disease course), ophthalmologic (Kayser-Fleischer rings and sunflower cataracts) and occasionally endocrinologic, cardiologic, or/or osteoskeletal. Kayser-Fleischer rings are green-blue corneal deposits.
reference: Litwin T et al. Psychiatric manifestations in Wilson’s disease: possibilities and difficulties for treatment. Therapeutic advances in psychopharmacology. 2018 Jul;8(7):199-211. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 166.

stem: Which of the following is preserved in associative visual agnosia?
explanation: Neurologic conditions such as strokes and other focal lesions have facilitated the definition of several disorders of visual perception. Apperceptive visual agnosia is the inability to identify and draw items using visual cues, with preservation of other sensory modalities. It represents failure of transmission of information from the higher visual sensory pathway to the association areas and is caused by bilateral lesions in the visual association areas. Associative visual agnosia is the inability to name or use objects despite the ability to draw them. It is caused by bilateral medial occipitotemporal lesions and can occur along with other visual impairments.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 927.

stem: A 76-year-old man is brought to the emergency unit by his wife. He had breakfast that morning, but appeared unable to remember that he and his wife had planned a day out. He repeatedly enquired where she was taking him. She reports that he appeared bewildered, but was alert and had no sensory and motor deficits throughout. He returned to a normal mental state after 10 hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The fundamental clinical feature of transient global amnesia (TGA) is the acute onset of amnesia. During an attack, patients cannot memorise or learn new information, that is, they have anterograde amnesia. They also cannot recall information acquired very recently, such as the events in the last several hours or days (i.e., they also have retrograde amnesia). Most patients seem calm but bewildered. TGA lasts for 3 to 24 hours but is most severe during the initial 1-2 hours. By definition, the total duration must not exceed 24 hours.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. p. 113.

stem: Diagnostic features of chronic fatigue syndrome include all of the following except:
explanation:
Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a debilitating disease with core symptoms of fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, post-exertional malaise, and cognitive dysfunction. The aetiology of the illness has yet to be revealed, which has led to no established objective diagnostics, pathophysiology, or therapeutics. Accordingly, many expert groups have developed case definitions based on clinical features. To date, over 20 ME/CFS case definitions have been established by different groups in various countries. The most widely used

have been the Fukuda criteria and the international criteria. A case of ME/CFS is defined by the presence of an unexplained, persistent, and relapsing chronic fatigue of new onset that is not alleviated by rest, which results in a significant reduction in the quality of life, and a concurrent occurrence of four or more of the following eight symptoms that must have persisted during six or more consecutive months: 1) ‘Brain fog’ – described as impairment in short-term memory or concentration severe enough to cause a reduction in previous levels of personal activities 2) Sore throat 3) Tender cervical or axillary nodes 4) Muscle pain 5) Multipoint pain without joint swelling

6) Headaches 7) Unrefreshing sleep 8) Post-exertional malaise lasting more than 24 hours
reference: Lim EJ, Son CG. Review of case definitions for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). Journal of translational medicine. 2020 Dec;18(1):1-10. Cortes Rivera M et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: a comprehensive review. Diagnostics. 2019 Sep;9(3):91.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has a history of 2 episodes of unilateral blindness that lasted for few weeks. She now presents with paraesthesia of the left leg. An MRI shows multiple demyelinating plaques. Which of the following is correct with respect to her illness?
options: It has a uniform, progressive course
It is due to a bacterial infection
It presents with diverse physical signs
It is more common in men than women
It occurs more commonly near the equator
correctAnswer: It presents with diverse physical signs
explanation: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated demyelinating disease. The cause is uncertain, but likely due to environmental factors (e.g. Epstein-Barr virus infection, vitamin D deficiency, latitude, and smoking) interacting with genetic predisposition. MS is twice as common in women as in men. It is seen with greater frequency as the distance from the equator increases (i.e. in White populations living in northern latitudes). It is characterized by multiple demyelinating lesions with a predilection for the optic nerves, cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord. MS is predominantly a white matter disease. Diverse physical signs reflect the presence and distribution of plaques. 85-90% of cases start with episode of acute neurological symptoms (e.g. optic neuritis). Most patients follow a relapsing-remitting course.
reference: Ron MA. The neuropsychiatry of multiple sclerosis. BJPsych Advances. 2018 May;24(3):178-87.

stem: Which of the following is a feature of sleep terrors?
options: Vivid memory of dreams on waking up
explanation: Sleep terrors are recurrent episodes of abrupt awakening from sleep characterised by a panicky scream, with intense fear and autonomic arousal. The individual usually has no recall of the details of the event and is unresponsive to stimuli (e.g conversation) during the episode. Sleep terrors typically occur during the first third of the night, during slow-wave stage 3 of NREM sleep. Autonomic hyperactivity is manifested by tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis, flushed face, dilated pupils, agitation, tremulousness, and increased muscle tone. Episodes usually last for 5-10 minutes.
reference: Leung AK et al. Sleep terrors: an updated review. Current pediatric reviews. 2020 Aug 1;16(3):176-82. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 462.

stem: Which of the following is an example of subcortical dementia?
explanation: Cortical dementias consist of illnesses in which neuropsychologic signs of cortical dysfunction – typically aphasia, agnosia, and apraxia – accompany dementia. Because the brain’s subcortical areas are relatively untouched, patients remain alert, attentive, and ambulatory. Alzheimer disease serves as the prime example of a cortical dementia. In contrast, subcortical dementias are typified by affective change, and slowed mental processing, which overshadow cognitive impairment. Gait abnormalities constitute the other core feature. Prime examples are Parkinson disease, NPH, HIV-associated dementia, vascular cognitive impairment, and MS.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. p. 115. Shaik SS, Varma AR. Differentiating the dementias: a neurological approach. Progress in Neurology and Psychiatry. 2012 Jan;16(1):11-8.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has been referred by her dentist for a long history of facial tingling, numbness, nausea and temporomandibular joint pain. Her symptoms have been anatomically inconsistent, and the pain has tended to fluctuate. She has insisted on multiple investigations, which have shown no abnormalities. The most likely diagnosis is
explanation: In ICD-11, bodily distress disorder has replaced the somatoform disorders of ICD-10. Bodily distress disorder is characterised by the presence of bodily symptoms that are distressing to the individual and excessive attention toward the symptoms, which may be manifest by repeated contact with health care providers. Bodily symptoms are persistent, being present on most days for at least several months. Typically, bodily distress disorder involves multiple bodily symptoms that may vary over time. Occasionally there is a single symptom – usually pain or fatigue – that is associated with the other features of the disorder. The symptoms and associated distress and preoccupation have at least some impact on the individual’s functioning.

stem: Which of the following are commonly seen in patients with post-concussion syndrome?
options: Short term memory loss and personality changes
Dizziness, headaches, irritability, and slowed information processing
correctAnswer: Dizziness, headaches, irritability, and slowed information processing
explanation: Post-concussion syndrome is characterised by one or more core symptoms – headache, memory impairment, and insomnia – lasting more than 2 to 3 months after a head injury. These and other symptoms of post-concussion syndrome – including irritability, sleepiness, tinnitus – remain entirely subjective and often nonspecific, variable, and occasionally unending. Patients with post-concussion syndrome characteristically describe mild amnesia accompanied by inattention or easy distractibility, slowed information processing, and difficulty completing complex mental tasks. Post-concussion syndrome patients also often report dizziness. In most cases, the dizziness is not authentic vertigo, but a nonspecific sensation with variable, idiosyncratic meanings that substitutes for lightheadedness, anxiety, unsteadiness, or lassitude. Patients have a normal physical and neurologic examination, CT, and MRI. Although the EEG may show minor abnormalities, the changes are generally inconsistent, insignificant, and often attributable to medications.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. pp. 559-560.

stem: A geriatric patient had a stroke 8 months ago. He now presents with retardation, amotivation, and anhedonia. He does not have any tearfulness or guilt. His MMSE score is 22/30 and he has executive dysfunction. What is his most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The vascular depression hypothesis postulates that cerebrovascular disease may predispose, precipitate, or perpetuate some geriatric depressive syndromes. Neurological signs and/or neurological findings, usually executive dysfunction, are found in most patients with vascular depression depending on the location and extent of lesions. Patients with vascular depression often present with retardation, anhedonia, lack of insight into their illness, and disability. They are less likely to report feelings of guilt.
reference: Alexopoulos GS. Mechanisms and treatment of late-life depression. Translational psychiatry. 2019 Aug 5;9(1):188.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is 6 months pregnant. She is depressed, has a previous history of depression, and a family history of depression. She has responded well to paroxetine in the past. If she were to take paroxetine for the remainder of her pregnancy, which of the following effects is most likely to be seen in the newborn?
explanation: SSRIs do not appear to be major teratogens, with most data supporting the safety of fluoxetine. When taken late in pregnancy, SSRIs may increase the risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn; the absolute risk is very low. Women who take SSRIs may be at increased risk of postpartum haemorrhage. The neonate may experience discontinuation symptoms, which are usually mild (such as agitation or irritability), or rarely respiratory distress and convulsions, with SSRIs. The risk is particularly high with short half-life drugs such as paroxetine and venlafaxine.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 685-689.

stem: A 21-year-old woman has been diagnosed with postpartum depression and is currently receiving antidepressant treatment. Which observer rating would be most appropriate to use to assess her response to treatment?

stem: Which of the following is correct with regard to the mechanism of action of modafinil?
options: It inhibits noradrenaline in the hypothalamus
It reduces dopamine in the nucleus accumbens
It activates neurons that release orexin
correctAnswer: It activates neurons that release orexin
explanation: Exactly how modafinil works is unknown, but it is clearly different from classical stimulants such as methylphenidate and amphetamine. Blockade of the dopamine transporter (DAT) by modafinil leads to increased tonic dopaminergic firing and downstream effects on wake- promoting neurotransmitters. Specifically, cortical release of wake-promoting neurotransmitters is increased, which leads to downstream release of histamine from the tuberomammillary nucleus and further activation of the lateral hypothalamus, with corresponding orexin release that stabilises wakefulness. Modafinil activates hypothalamic neurons that release orexin/hypocretin. The elimination half-life of modafinil is 10-12 hours.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber’s Guide, 7th Edition. 2021. pp. 521-523. Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. p. 445.

stem: Which of the following antidepressants has an effect in common with anti-nausea drugs such as ondansetron?
explanation: Mirtazapine has 5HT3 antagonism action. The 5HT3 receptors best known to clinicians are perhaps those localised in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the brainstem - where they mediate nausea and vomiting, especially in response to cancer chemotherapy - and also those localised in the gastrointestinal tract itself - where they mediate nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea/bowel motility when stimulated by serotonin. Blocking these 5HT3 receptors can therefore protect against chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting as well as against serotonin-induced gastrointestinal side effects that can accompany agents that increase serotonin. Oral disintegrating tablets of mirtazapine have been used peri-operatively for nausea.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5th Edition. 2021. pp. 309-311. Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 891.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with a history of bipolar disorder is currently breastfeeding her child. She has a manic relapse, though the presentation is not severe enough to warrant hospitalisation. What would be the best medication to treat her relapse?
explanation:
Maudsley prescribing guidelines advises us to refrain from using any mood stabilisers if at all possible in breast feeding mothers. If necessary one may use valproate. Treatment of bipolar disorder invariably requires mood stabilizers, lorazepam and chloral hydrate can be safely excluded. Maternal use of lithium and carbamazepine has been associated with serious difficulties in babies. Lithium increases the

risk of thyroid dysfunction, cyanosis, poor muscle tone, and ECG changes in infants. Also renal clearance is decreased in infants up to at least 5 months of age, so the use of lithium during breastfeeding is not advisable unless the mother was already on lithium and discontinuation led to severe relapse not treatable by any other drug. In this case both infant and mother's lithium levels need monitoring. There has been a single recorded case of serious blood abnormalities following exposure to sodium valproate through breast milk, and hepatotoxicity can occur when valproate is directly administered to infants. Therefore, when administering valproate to breastfeeding mothers, pediatric clinical status, liver enzymes, and platelets should be carefully monitored. Carbamazepine can cause hepatic dysfunction and so it is advisable to monitor liver enzymes, bilirubin, and WBC counts frequently and to assay for carbamazepine levels in exposed infants. There is limited, though reassuring data on lamotrigine and no data for the use of gabapentin by nursing mothers. But these agents are not first-line medications for bipolar disorder. Burt et al. (2001) The use of psychotropic medication during breastfeeding. Am J Psychiatry 158:1001-1009.

explanation: Explanation Herpes simplex encephalitis causes amnesia accompanied by personality changes, focal impaired awareness seizures (previously named complex partial seizures), and the Kluver-Bucy syndrome because the virus typically enters the undersurface of the brain through the nasopharynx and preferentially attacks the temporal lobes. This condition occurs relatively frequently because herpes simplex is the most common cause of sporadically occurring (non-epidemic) viral encephalitis. In contrast, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) encephalitis does not cause this picture.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. p. 112.

stem: Which of the following occurs in Ganser syndrome?
explanation: Ganser syndrome is characterised by approximate answers, disorientation, clouding of consciousness, hallucinations/pseudo-hallucinations, motor disturbance, anxiety or apathy, normal ADLs, and sudden resolution with amnesia for the period of illness. In ICD-11, it is included under ‘other specified dissociative disorders’.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 236. Dieguez S. Ganser syndrome. Neurologic-Psychiatric Syndromes in Focus-Part II. 2018;42:1-22.

stem: A patient with bipolar disorder and a history of mixed affective states is in the first trimester of her pregnancy. She has not been on any medications of late, but is very concerned about the possibility of relapse. Of the following, what would be the preferred medication to prescribe to her?
explanation: For pregnant women with bipolar disorder who have had a long period without relapse, the possibility of switching to a safer drug (antipsychotic) or withdrawing treatment completely before conception and for at least the first trimester should be considered. No mood stabiliser is clearly safe. NICE recommends the use of mood stabilising antipsychotics as a preferable alternative to a mood stabiliser.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 692.

stem: Which one of the following medications could be used to treat pathologic crying?
explanation: The most conspicuous feature of pseudobulbar palsy is emotional lability. With little or no provocation, patients tend to burst into tears or, less often, laughter, with no apparent change in their mood. These unprovoked emotional expressions are referred to as pathologic laughing and crying, pseudobulbar affect, or involuntary emotional expression disorder. Amitriptyline, SSRIs (such as citalopram), or a combination of dextromethorphan and quinidine may suppress this.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9th Edition. 2023. p. 39.

stem: A pregnant bipolar patient has no other treatment option but to continue valproate. Which of the following should she take in addition?
explanation: Valproate is an established human teratogen. Usually, valproate should be reserved for post-menopausal women only. Its use in younger women should be treatment of last resort. There is no evidence that folate protects against anticonvulsant-induced neural tube defects if given during pregnancy, but may do so if given prior to conception (the neural tube is essentially formed by 8 weeks of pregnancy before many women realise they are pregnant). However, folate supplementation may be beneficial for early neurodevelopment and so should always be offered.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 260, 680, 691.

stem: What would be the most appropriate drug for a depressed lady who is pregnant?
explanation: Fluoxetine has the most evidence and is safer than paroxetine. Other drugs recommended by Maudlsey guidelines include Amitryptyline, Nortryptyline and Imipramine. (Maudsley guidelines- 10th edition pg 354)

stem: Which of the following favours psychogenic nonepileptic seizures rather than epileptic seizures?
explanation: Ictal eye closure has been assessed in several controlled studies and is significantly more frequent in psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES) than epileptic seizures (ES). Closed eyes during an attack is considered a discriminator between PNES and ES. The mean duration of PNES is longer than ES. There is considerable evidence to suggest that a duration of more than 2 minutes is highly suggestive of PNES, although this is an arbitrary limit. Duration of longer than 10 minutes strongly suggests PNES. In studies that have compared convulsive PNES with generalised tonic clonic seizures, the proportion of events with side-to-side head or body movement, especially with coordinated agonist and antagonist activity, are significantly higher in PNES.
reference: Xiang X et al. Differential diagnosis between epileptic seizures and psychogenic nonepileptic seizures based on semiology. Acta Epileptologica. 2019 Dec;1(1):1-5.

stem: Idiopathic progressive calcium deposition in the basal ganglia is seen in
explanation: Fahr disease, also known as idiopathic basal ganglia calcification, is a rare autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder, characterised by bilateral calcifications in multiple basal ganglia. Patients with Fahr disease may be asymptomatic or present with movement disorders such as parkinsonism, psychiatric disorders such as psychosis and depression, cognitive impairment, dementia, and a variety of other symptoms. The age on onset is mostly between 40 and 50 years, but the symptoms can manifest at any age. Patients who become symptomatic early in adulthood mostly develop psychiatric or cognitive disorders, like psychosis, whereas patients who become symptomatic later in life develop mainly movement disorders in combination with other clinical features.
reference: Peters ME et al. Mechanisms of calcification in Fahr disease and exposure of potential therapeutic targets. Neurology: Clinical Practice. 2020 Oct 1;10(5):449-57.

explanation: Once effective treatment has been adequately delivered and adhered to, there will be a proportion of patients with anxiety that have not remitted and a smaller proportion that remain quite symptomatic. At this point, it should be considered whether there are exogenous factors that are aggravating and/or maintaining anxiety, whether there is a medical condition, and whether the diagnosis may be wrong or incomplete (i.e. whether there is a comorbidity present that is accounting for the poor response to treatment).
reference: Roy-Byrne P. Treatment-refractory anxiety; definition, risk factors, and treatment challenges. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2015 Jun;17(2):191.

reference: Meltzer-Brody S et al. Postpartum psychiatric disorders. Nature Reviews Disease Primers. 2018 Apr 26;4(1):1-8.

stem: The most common psychiatric symptom in Cushing syndrome is
explanation: Cushing syndrome is a relatively rare but serious condition that results from chronic hypercortisolism. Depression is the most prevalent and significant psychiatric disorder among patients with Cushing syndrome.

stem: Which of the following MRI findings is characteristically seen in Huntington disease?
explanation: Huntington disease is a rare neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervous system, with a genetic autosomal dominant inheritance, that first involves the basal ganglia (caudate nucleus and putamen) and results from expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT (huntingtin) gene. In Huntington disease, CT/MRI show atrophy of the basal ganglia (caudate and putamen) with ‘boxing’ of the caudate and dilatation of the ventricles.
reference: Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment of Huntington’s Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 166.

stem: Mr. Y has been treated for multiple sclerosis, and he developed depression following treatment. Which of the following drugs is most likely to have induced the depression?
explanation:
Beta and alpha interferons used in the treatment of multiple sclerosis is associated with depression. The role of beta interferons in the etiology of Multiple Sclerosis related depression is unclear. Standard care for initiation of beta interferon should include assessment for depression and for those with a past history of depressive illness, prophylactic treatment with an antidepressant is recommended (Ref: The

Maudsley prescribing guidelines; 10th edition; pg 410)

stem: A 45-year-old man with diabetes is brought to the emergency department with nausea, vomiting, lethargy, and muscle cramps. He has been diagnosed with depression and recently started on fluoxetine. What is the most likely metabolic complication?
explanation: Most antidepressants have been associated with hyponatraemia. The most likely mechanism of this adverse effect is the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). There is a strong level of supporting evidence that SSRIs (including fluoxetine) are associated with a relatively high risk of hyponatraemia. All patients taking antidepressants should be informed of and observed for signs of hyponatraemia (dizziness, nausea, lethargy, confusion, cramps, seizures).
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 393-394.

stem: Which of the following is an effective treatment for post-stroke depression based on the best available evidence?
explanation: A metaanalysis that pooled 385 patients from 6 trials published through December 2009 that evaluated the prophylactic efficacy of fluoxetine in poststroke patients. They found that fluoxetine reduced the incidence of poststroke depression, helped recovery in neurologic function, and improved independence in activities of daily living.

explanation: .'Trance and possession' disorders are placed under the general rubric of dissociative disorder (ICD-10) implying a psychological causation of symptoms. Possession is characterized by a transient alteration in identity whereby one's normal identity is temporarily replaced or possessed by a spirit, ghost, deity, etc. This disorder may be culture-bound for some non-Western cultures.

stem: 'Baby blues' are reported in what proportion of new mothers?
explanation: Baby blues: Up to 3/4 of new mothers will experience a short-lived period of tearfulness and emotional lability starting two or three days after birth and lasting one to two days. This is common enough to be easily recognizable by midwifery staff and requires only reassurance and observation towards resolution. There is weak evidence that it may be related to post-partum reductions in levels of oestrogen, progesterone, and prolactin (which do occur around 72 hrs after the birth). Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry; 756

stem: Doctor-shopping is an entity associated with which psychiatric condition?
explanation:
Somatisation disorder: "Diagnosis is usually only suspected after negative findings begin to emerge as normal medical practice is to take complaints at face value. Key diagnostic feature is multiple, atypical, and inconsistent medically unexplained symptoms in a patient under the age of 40. There is excessive use of medical service and alternative therapies. Chronic cases will have had large numbers of diagnostic procedures and surgical or medical treatments. High risk of iatrogenic harm and iatrogenic substance dependence. Hostility and frustration

can be felt on both sides of the doctor-patient relationship. There may be doctor-shopping and splitting of the attitudes of staff caring for them. Psychological approaches to treatment are hampered by on-going investigations of ever rarer diagnostic possibilities and by the attribution of symptoms to fictitious but named medical entities". (Excerpt from Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry; 744)

stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect about somatisation disorder?
options: Most frequent symptoms are non specific and atypical
It is associated with significant psychological distress and functional impairment
Usually presents before the age of 40
Symptoms are usually localised to a single physiological system
Usually have long complex medical histories
correctAnswer: Symptoms are usually localised to a single physiological system
explanation:
Somatisation disorder is a chronic disorder of multiple medically unexplained symptoms, affecting multiple organ systems presenting before the age of 40. It is associated with significant psychological distress, functional impairment, and repeated presentations to medical services. Full blown somatisation disorder or Briquet's syndrome probably represents the severe end of a continuum of abnormal illness behaviour (Excerpt from Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry). Patients will have long, complex medical histories, although at interview may minimize all but

the most recent symptomatology.

explanation: Risk of suicide within one year of DSH - 0.7% (nearly 1 in 100); more in males 1.1%; 0.5% in females. This is 66 x the general population risk. Roughly 1% will die by completed suicide in the 24 months after the initial parasuicidal act, with the risk highest in the weeks following the original act. stem: Which one among the following is not an observation normally associated with Herpes simplex encephalitis?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the imaging of choice in HSE
Gold standard for in vivo diagnosis is CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for herpes viruses.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination commonly reveals a lymphocytosis and a raised protein
The EEG is invariably abnormal in HSE.
CT Scan usually reveals signal change and swelling within the frontal lobes
correctAnswer: CT Scan usually reveals signal change and swelling within the frontal lobes
explanation:
Investigatory findings observed in patients with Herpes simplex encephalitis: Neuroimaging usually reveals signal change and swelling within the temporal lobes; this is often visible on CT, but is more easily seen using MRI. Significant brain swelling may lead to raised intracranial pressure. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination commonly reveals a lymphocytosis and raised protein, Gold standard for in vivo diagnosis is CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for herpes viruses, which has a sensitivity and specificity of ~95%. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

provides the most sensitive method of detecting early lesions and is the imaging of choice in HSE. The EEG is invariably abnormal in HSE. "Non-specific slowing may be the only feature early in the illness; the later stages are more likely to be associated with high voltage periodic lateralising epileptiform discharges"(Retrieved from http://jnnp.bmj.com/content/73/3/237.full.pdf). If present they are diagnostically useful but they are not specific for HSE.

stem: Most cases of herpes simplex encephalitis are caused by
explanation: In children older than 3 months and in adults, HSE is usually localized to the temporal and frontal lobes and is caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). In neonates, however, brain involvement is generalized, and the usual cause is herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), which is acquired at the time of delivery (Herpes Simplex Encephalitis: HSE - Medscape Reference. Retrieved from http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1165183-overview).

stem: A woman who has had Herpes encephalitis develops severe carbohydrate craving, weight gain and inappropriate sexuality. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Herpes simplex encephalitis: HSE is the most common cause of Kluver Bucy syndrome in humans; this is characterized by emotional blunting, hyperphagia, visual agnosia and inappropriate sexual behaviour. This is due to bilateral temporal lobe damage and most often only a partial syndrome is evident. Carbamazepine may be used to control some symptoms.

stem: Which of the following statements about Meige's syndrome is incorrect?
options: The movement is present both at rest and when active
Oral facial dystonia characterized by repetitive blinking and chin thrusting
The patients are more likely to be middle-aged men than women
correctAnswer: The patients are more likely to be middle-aged men than women
explanation:
Henri Meige described in 1904 a new type of oral facial dystonia characterized by repetitive blinking and chin thrusting. Some patients have lip pursing or tongue movements and, for a few, the movements spread into the shoulders. Primary Meige's is idiopathic; antipsychotics, levodopa and Lewy body dementia can cause secondary Meige's. At times there is a joint interactive movement between the oral movements and the eye movements. The patients are more likely to be women than men and usually at middle age. There is some variation

with stress, but the movement is present both at rest and when active; it disappears with sleep. Patients may chew gum, whistle or touch their face in an effort to lessen the movements (Retrieved from http://www.blepharospasm.org/meiges-syndrome1.html).

stem: Which one of the following is a weak inhibitor of cytochrome P450 enzyme system?
explanation: Fluoxetine and Paroxetine are potent inhibitors of hepatic CYP enzyme systems (CYP2D6, CYP3A4). Sertraline is a less potent inhibitor but this effect is dose related; at higher doses that are commonly used in practice, sertraline may induce clinically important inhibition of the CYP system. Citalopram is a weak inhibitor. Ref: Maudsley prescribing guidelines, 10th edition; 336

stem: Some patients intentionally falsify their symptoms and past history and fabricate signs of physical or mental disorder with the primary aim of obtaining medical attention and treatment. Which of the following diagnosis is most appropriate in these circumstances?
explanation:
Factitious disorder (Munchausen's Syndrome): In factitious disorder patients intentionally falsify their symptoms and past history and fabricate signs of physical or mental disorder with the primary aim of obtaining medical attention and treatment. The diagnostic features are the intentional and conscious production of signs, falsification, or exaggeration of the history and the lack of gain beyond medical attention

and treatment.

stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor associated with depression in Parkinson's disease?
explanation: Depression in Parkinson's disease: Risk factors include Female sex, younger onset, prominent right-sided signs, bradykinesia and gait disturbance, rapid disease progression, poorer cognitive status and activities of daily living. Apathy without depression is also common and is associated with executive dysfunction. It may be masked by Parkinsonian affect - subjective exploration may be necessary.

stem: All are true about delirium in palliative care except
options: Occurs in over 50% of patients at some stage in their illness
explanation: Delirium is common in palliative care settings. The prevalence is around 44% in cancer in-patients, rising to 62% shortly before death. It may be either hypoactive sedated subtype or hyperactive agitated type. The aetiology is usually multi-factorial, and a specific aetiology is discovered in less than 50% of terminally ill patients with delirium. Though small dose of haloperidol or lorazepam is frequently used, they are not always successful in controlling the symptoms, especially in sedated subtype.

options: Long period of post traumatic amnesia
Long duration of loss of consciousness
Focal damage restricted to the non-dominant lobe
correctAnswer: Focal damage restricted to the non-dominant lobe
explanation: After a head injury, patients who struggle to return to previous activities generally report a longer duration of post-traumatic amnesia and loss of consciousness than those who resume work without much difficulties. Focal non-dominant lobe damage does not indicate poor prognosis.

explanation: Addison's disease: (Cortisol depletion) Psychiatric symptoms - apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, and depressed mood. May be misdiagnosed as major depressive disorder. Anorexia is common in both, but the presence of nausea, vomiting and skin changes (dark pigmentation in some) should suggest Addison's disease.

stem: A proportion of patients who are at a high risk of HIV are seronegative but remain anxious about contracting HIV. Which of the following descriptions/diagnosis suits them best?

Some of the charactersitics of the worried well include: Several negative HIV tests Poor sexual adjustment and social isolation Multiple somatic features wrongly interpreted as a part of an undiagnosed HIV illness Psychiatric history - especially anxiety or depression

Spuriously high diagnosis due to shared symptomatology
explanation: The risk factors for depression are similar to the risk factors for those without HIV. These include; A. advanced HIV infection: B. loss of social support; C. personal and family history of depression; D. drug use; and E. lack of confidants. Poor adherence to medical treatment for HIV can occur as a result of depression, complicating management. Antiretroviral therapy is not a common cause of depression.

stem: In patients with transient global amnesia, the amnesic episode usually resolves within
explanation: Transient global amnesia is characterized by the abrupt onset anterograde amnesia characterized by significant new learning deficit" (Excerpt from Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry). Patients show mild confusion and a lack of insight into the problem but an intact sensorium. Episodes last from 6 to 24 hours. Though the aetiology is unclear, most cases involve hypoperfusion in the temporal and parietotemporal regions, particularly in the left hemisphere. Most patients show complete improvement though recurrence is high.

Can be treated with cognitive behavioural therapy
Can be caused by the drugs used to treat the neurological condition

stem: Which one of the following cognitive faculties remains intact in amnestic disorders?
explanation:
The Amnestic disorders are syndromes characterised by the development of a memory disorder characterized by impairment in the ability to learn new information (anterograde amnesia) and the inability to recall previously remembered knowledge (retrograde amnesia). A general medical condition or use substance usually causes it, and where delirium and dementia have been excluded as causative of the amnesia. In amnesic disorders, short-term and recent memory is usually impaired. Memory for events from the remote past, such as

childhood experiences, is generally retained, but the memory for events from the less remote past (over the past decade) is impaired.

Can be explained by the increased prevalence of depression in multiple sclerosis
Has the same feature as a subcortical dementia
Is best screened for using the Mini-Mental State Examination

explanation:
Subcortical dementia is "a clinical syndrome characterized by slowness of mental processing, forgetfulness, impaired cognition, apathy, and depression. First recognized in progressive supranuclear palsy and Huntington's disease, the concept has been extended to account for the intellectual impairment of Parkinson's disease, Wilson's disease, spinocerebellar degenerations, idiopathic basal ganglia calcification, the lacunar state, and the dementia syndrome of MS"(Excerpt from Cummings, J. L., & Benson, D. F. (1984). Subcortical dementia: Review of an

emerging concept. Archives of Neurology, 41(8), 874-879.).

Psychosis is associated with decreases in antiparkinsonian medications
Quetiapine is best avoided among all antipsychotics

explanation: Psychiatric symptoms in epilepsy: Depression- 30-50%, Panic disorder- 20%, Psychosis- 3-7%

stem: A 42-year-old man suffering from poorly controlled epilepsy is referred by the neurologist as non-epileptic seizures are suspected. Which of the following statement is correct?

Prolactin levels are elevated after non-epileptic attack
Video recording of ictal and periictal behaviour can help in diagnosis
Known epileptic patients do not have dissociative seizures
Presence of depression suggests non-epileptic attacks in most epileptics.
correctAnswer: Video recording of ictal and periictal behaviour can help in diagnosis
explanation:
Pseudoseizures (Non epileptic seizures) are often associated with past psychiatric history. Pseudoseizures more likely to happen in the daytime and when others are present. Increased post-ictal serum prolactin concentrations (greater than 1000 IU/l) despite normal baseline levels are found after epileptic seizures but measurements must be taken within 15 min of the event. Video recording along with EEG is the

best diagnostic measure.

stem: Which one of the following drugs is particularly epileptogenic and should be used with caution in epileptic psychosis?
explanation: Prevalence of psychosis in epilepsy is between 3 and 7%. It is more common in those with partial epilepsies. Haloperidol and Sulpiride may be less epileptogenic than other antipsychotics and, therefore, the treatment of choice for epileptic psychosis. Clozapine can worsen epileptic psychosis by lowering seizure threshold.

stem: Post-traumatic epilepsy is seen in what proportion of patients with open head injury?
explanation: Post-traumatic epilepsy is seen in 5% closed and 30% open head injuries (usually during first year) and worsens prognosis. Less psychopathology in children after head injury due to increased brain plasticity.

stem: Post-concussional syndrome is characterized by all except;
explanation: Post-concussional syndrome is characterized by headache, dizziness, fatigue, poor memory, poor concentration, irritability, depression, sleep disturbance, frustration, restlessness, sensitivity to noise, blurred vision, double vision, photophobia, nausea and tinnitus (King, 1997). At least 50% experience some post-concussion symptoms that recover completely within 3 months of injury, except in nearly a third.

Predominant frontal distribution of plaques in MRI
Can be induced by prescribed treatments for multiple sclerosis
Can occur as part of the primary physical disorder.

stem: A 45-year-old gentleman was admitted to the medical unit with history of stroke. A psychiatric opinion was requested due to his deteriorating mental state. His MRI brain scan showed lesions proximal to the left frontal lobe. Which one of the following psychiatric conditions is most likely to occur in this scenario?
explanation: According to a meta-analytic study by Narushima et, al. 2003, the proximity of the lesions to the left frontal lobe predicts depressive illness. This is also supported by another study from Finland (Vataja et al. 2004).

stem: Which of the following statements about mania in multiple sclerosis is incorrect?
options: There is MRI evidence suggesting that patients showing mania with psychotic symptoms have plaques that are distributed
predominantly in the bilateral temporal horn areas
Mild to moderate degrees of mania seen in up to 2/3rd of patients given steroids.
Higher than expected prevalence of mania
People with multiple sclerosis who become hypomanic on steroid therapy are more likely to have a family history of affective disorder.
correctAnswer: Mild to moderate degrees of mania seen in up to 2/3rd of patients given steroids.
explanation:
Mania in multiple sclerosis: Higher than expected prevalence of mania. It can also be drug induced: steroids (more likely), baclofen, dantrolene, tizanidine (central muscle relaxant). Mild to moderate degrees of mania seen in up to 1/3rd of patients given steroids. People with multiple sclerosis who become hypomanic on steroid therapy are more likely to have a family or premorbid history of affective disorder

and/or alcoholism. There is MRI evidence suggesting that patients showing mania with psychotic symptoms have plaques that are distributed predominantly in the bilateral temporal horn areas

stem: What is the lifetime prevalence of depressive symptoms in patients with multiple sclerosis?
explanation: In patients with multiple sclerosis, lifetime prevalence of depressive symptoms is reported in 40-50%. It is about three times higher than the rate in the general population. Desipramine and SSRIs have an evidence base for their use in the treatment. ECT may be used. However, there is a 20% risk of triggering a relapse of multiple sclerosis if ECT is given

stem: A 65-year-old gentleman with Parkinson's disease presented with psychotic symptoms characterized by paranoia and visual hallucinations. His wife does not want his antiparkinsonian medication to be stopped as it has worsened the motor features of Parkinsons disease in the past. Which antipsychotic can improve his symptoms without worsening Parkinsonism?
explanation:
In parkinsonian psychosis, consideration should be given to decreasing or stopping antiparkinsonian drugs. Due to the propensity to cause EPSEs antipsychotic medications should be used with caution. There is good evidence that low dose clozapine (less than 100 mg/day) can

improve psychosis without worsening parkinsonism (Parkinson study group 1999).

stem: The gene for Huntington's disease (HD) is located on which chromosome?
explanation: Huntington's disease can manifest at any time between infancy and senescence. The mutant protein in Huntington's disease—huntingtin— results from an expanded CAG repeat leading to a polyglutamine strand of variable length at the N-terminus. This tail confers a toxic gain of function. The gene for Huntington's disease (HD) is located on the short arm of chromosome four and is associated with an expanded trinucleotide repeat.

stem: Head injury may predispose to the development of
explanation:
Head injuries, particularly in men, may predispose to the development of Alzheimers disease. (Fleminger et al 2003). It is possibly due to deposition of beta amyloid in the brain at the time of the injury, although evidence that it is linked to APOE status is inconsistent. Head injury has long been considered as a possible risk factor for schizophrenia although a comprehensive critical review of psychosis following head injury concludes that the injury is unlikely to be a causal factor in the disorder (David and Prince 2005; Advances in neuropsychiatry: clinical

implications | BJPsych. Retrieved from http://apt.rcpsych.org/content/12/1/23). Nevertheless, 'psychosis' is known to occur after head injuries.

explanation: Depressive illness after stroke is extremely common, occurring in up to 50-60% of cases. Its onset is usually between 3 and 24 months following the stroke.

stem: Mrs. Z has a history of epilepsy and has now been diagnosed with depression. Which class of drugs should be used as first a line treatment in her case?
explanation: Depression in epilepsy is mainly associated with the location of lesion - esp. common in TLE. High risk of suicide is present in epilepsy even without depression; mortality shoots when clinical depression is positive (nearly 25 times higher). SSRIs are the first line; may reduce seizure threshold but rare. Lithium can increase seizure severity and reduces the seizure threshold.

stem: Lesions caused by an injury to which part of the brain predicts depression?
explanation: Depression (most common sequelae) and anxiety occur in roughly 1/4 of head injury survivors. Meta-analysis shows that proximity of lesion to left frontal lobe predicts depression. Suicide risk is also higher post head injury. A schizophrenia-like psychosis with prominent paranoia is associated with left temporal injury, while affective psychoses (esp. mania in 9% patients) are associated with right temporal or orbitofrontal injury. There is also an increased prevalence of schizophrenia post head injury (-2.5% develop the disorder).

stem: Which of the following is a risk factor associated with cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease?
explanation:
Cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease: It is Common; poor prognosis if present at time of initial referral. Ranges from mild to severe dementia syndrome. Risk factors are Older patients, late-onset Parkinson's disease, low socio-economic status, low education and severe extrapyramidal signs. Lewy body dementia is closely linked pathologically; rivastigmine is useful in LBD. No drugs licensed yet for Parkinson related dementia. Neuroleptic sensitivity is seen. Higher incidence of hallucination and delusions than Alzheimer's. Frontal executive

dysfunction - a subcortical pattern is seen.

stem: Concerning movement disorders in Parkinson's disease all are true except
options: They may be aggravated by psychotropic medication
Levodopa causes dose dependent psychiatric manifestations
Presence of cognitive impairment improves prognosis
correctAnswer: Presence of cognitive impairment improves prognosis
explanation:
Almost all patients with PD suffer from selective cognitive impairments, including difficulties with attention, concentration, problem solving, set-shifting, and memory, which are thought to reflect dysfunction of cortical circuits subserving frontal brain regions. These impairments are most frequently reported by patients in terms of the disabilities they cause, such as difficulties in paying attention at work; problems handling more than one project at a time; inability to sequence, plan, and organize tasks at work and home; and problems completing tasks

that have been started. These disabilities present serious complications for patients in the management of their everyday lives, particularly with regard to occupational functioning(Cognitive Impairment in Parkinson's Disease - Primary Psychiatry. Retrieved from http://primarypsychiatry.com/cognitive-impairment-in-parkinsonas-disease/).

stem: Huntington's disease is transmitted through which of the following genetic changes?
options: Autosomal recessive gene on the short arm of chromosome 4
Autosomal dominant gene on the short arm of chromosome 4
Autosomal recessive gene on the short arm of chromosome 4
Autosomal dominant gene on the long arm of chromosome 4
X-linked recessive gene on the short arm of chromosome 4
correctAnswer: Autosomal dominant gene on the short arm of chromosome 4
explanation: A single autosomal dominant gene on the short arm of chromosome 4 transmits Huntington's disease. There is Autosomal dominant inheritance with 100% penetrance; thus 50% of a patient's offspring will be affected. The specific genetic defect has been identified as an expansion of the trinucleotide sequence CAG between 37 and 120 repeats on chromosome 4.

stem: During pregnancy, where continued use of Valproate is deemed essential, what is the maximum dose recommended?
explanation: Where continued use of Valproate or carbamazepine is deemed essential, low dose monotherapy is strongly recommended, as the teratogenic effect is probably dose related. NICE recommends that the dose of Valproate should be limited to 1000 mg a day. Ref: Maudsley prescribing guidelines, 10th edition; 351

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: When used as mood stabilizers, what is the minimum period suggested to withdraw anticonvulsant drugs?
explanation: When used as mood stabilizers, it would be prudent to withdraw anticonvulsant drugs slowly. The optimum period of taper is unknown. A period of at least 1 month is suggested. When used for epilepsy, the dose should be gradually tapered over a period of 6 months. If the patient is taking more than one anticonvulsant, each drug should be withdrawn sequentially. Ref: Maudsley prescribing guidelines, 10th edition; 343

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: What is the lifetime risk of suicide in Huntington's disease?
explanation: The suicide rate for patients with Huntington's disease is 4-6 times higher than that for the general population, being as high as 12.7%, and increasing further in those over the age of 50. Suicide is reported to be the 3rd common cause of death after pneumonia and cardiovascular disease in patients with Huntington's disease.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: What is the most common behavioural change observed in patients with Huntington's disease?
explanation:
The high prevalence of behavioral problems in patients with Huntington's disease was first recorded by Craufurd et al. in 2001. The most common behavioral change observed in patients with Huntington's disease is lack of initiative followed by poor judgement, blunting of affect, poor self-care, self-centeredness and inflexibility. Irritability, impulsivity and verbal outbursts are also reported ranging from 15 to 60% of cases. Ref: Craufurd D Thompson JC Snowden (2001); behavioral change in Huntington's disease. Neuropsychiatry and behavioral

neurology; 14: 219-226

stem: Which of the following feature is associated more with Huntington's rather than Alzheimer's dementia?
options: Impairment in executive function correlates with general cognitive decline
explanation:
Sub cortical type of dementia is seen in Huntington's and cortical type is seen in Alzheimer's type. All the other features listed above are more associated with Alzheimer's type. Other features of Huntington's include gradual onset, early and significant impairment in executive function, disproportionate to other cognitive domains, language function relatively preserved until late, Visuospatial function and semantic memory relatively preserved until late. The predominant cognitive impairment in Huntington's disease is characterized by impaired

executive function.

stem: Choose an accurate statement with regard to depressive disorders in terminal illness
options: Presence of somatic symptoms strongly favour the diagnosis
It does not respond to antidepressants
Depression is uncommon in palliative care settings
explanation: SSRIs do not have much evidence but are widely used in depressed patients receiving palliative care. Low dose amitriptyline (avoid in delirium risk; useful if neuropathic pain), lofepramine and rapid-acting psychostimulant such as dexamphetamine or methylphenidate (in a patient who has only weeks of life) are other useful options.

stem: Which of the following tests would be required to make a diagnosis of Huntington's disease in a patient without a family history?
explanation: Sporadic appearance of new mutations is not uncommon in the Huntington disease gene. Hence a genetic test is advised even in those who present without family history.

stem: Mr. P has treatment resistant schizophrenia and is currently on clozapine 600 mg /day. Which anticonvulsant should be used to prevent clozapine induced seizures?
explanation: Sodium Valproate is the anticonvulsant of choice as it has a lower incidence of leucopenia than carbamazepine.

stem: Which of the following statements about periodic limb movement disorders (PLMD) is incorrect?
options: Its diagnosis requires polysomnographic documentation of an increased number of PLMS in association with significant disruption of
PLMS are a common phenomenon in otherwise healthy individuals.
These movements can cause clinical sleep disturbance expressed by insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness.
It is characterized by periodic episodes of repetitive and stereotyped limb movements that occur during sleep.
explanation:
PLMD is characterized by periodic episodes of repetitive and stereotyped limb movements that occur during sleep. These movements can cause clinical sleep disturbance expressed by insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness. In contrast to RLS, PLMD is not an awake phenomenon but an asleep phenomenon, and its diagnosis requires polysomnographic documentation of an increased number of PLMS in

association with significant disruption of sleep architecture and symptomatology. Polysomnographic diagnostic criteria for PLMS1 are based on electromyography (EMG) of the right and left anterior tibialis muscles. The movements may or may not be followed by arousal or awakening as determined by the polysomnogram. PLMS are a common phenomenon in otherwise healthy individuals. They also become more prevalent with increasing age (occurring in up to 34% of people over 60 years of age).

stem: Many patients with Chronic Fatigue Syndrome will meet the criteria for another psychiatric diagnosis, which is most commonly;
explanation:
Many patients with CFS will meet the criteria for another psychiatric diagnosis, most commonly major depression. Arguments exist for calling CFS a form of atypical depression; however this is untenable in a significant minority of cases. Not only do patients resist a 'psychiatric' diagnosis, but many do not have anhedonia or pervasively low mood, and attribute any mood disturbance to the restriction on their activities caused by their illness. Nonetheless, treatment of co morbid depressive or anxiety symptoms can produce clinical

improvement. There is a high rate of depression in patient with CFS. 23% of CFS patient have current major depression and 50%- 75% have life time history of major depression (Wessley et .al, 1998 ). Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry-753

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Liaison Part 2_ Attempt review.pdf

stem: A 75-year-old man with Parkinsons disease develops psychosis unrelated to levodopa use. Choose the best antipsychotic:
explanation: Eight open-label studies have assessed quetiapine use in 191 patients with psychosis and Parkinson's disease, with improvement in psychosis recorded in 152 (80%). In addition to the open-label studies, there have been two single-blind, randomized trials comparing quetiapine and clozapine. These studies suggest that quetiapine has similar efficacy to clozapine in controlling psychosis.

stem: Which of the following factors have been implicated in the generation of periodic limb movement disorders?
explanation: Dopaminergic impairment and iron deficiency have been implicated in the generation of PLMS, similar to restless leg syndrome.

stem: Mrs.Z has a history of bipolar depression and is on treatment with mood stabilizer throughout her pregnancy. She gave birth to a male child with Cleft palate. The most likely offending drug is;
explanation: Data for Lamotrigine suggests a low risk of foetal malformation when used as monotherapy, although a substantially increased risk of cleft palate has been reported. Clearance of Lamotrigine seems to increase radically during pregnancy. NICE suggest that Lamotrigine should not be routinely prescribed in pregnancy.

stem: The core symptom of neurasthenia is
explanation:
Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) is the current preferred name for a clinical syndrome whose central feature is severe fatigue, unrelated to exertion and unrelieved by rest (neurasthenia). Fatigue is a symptom characterised by a subjective feeling of lethargy, lack of energy, exhaustion, and a feeling of increased effort to do anything. Patients also complain of aching muscles, poor unrefreshing sleep, aching joints, and headaches. They may date the symptoms very precisely to an episode of viral infection with sore throat, fever, and tender lymph

nodes. CFS is currently preferred to the names myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME) and post-viral fatigue syndrome as it doesn't imply knowledge of underlying pathology or aetiology. Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry-754.

stem: Mr. Q suffers from epilepsy and psychosis with paranoid delusions and auditory hallucination. He is worried about metabolic side effects of newer antipsychotics and would like to take an older antipsychotic medication. The drug that should be avoided in his case would be;
explanation: Chlorpromazine is the most epileptogenic of the older drugs and ideally should be avoided completely. Sulpiride, Haloperidol and Trifluoperazine have a low pro-convulsive effect and are a good choice for epileptic patients. Ref: Maudsley prescribing guidelines, 10th edition; 337
